questions.q: How many rows does a truth table need for an expression with three inputs?
questions.feedback: 2³ = 8. Each extra input doubles the number of rows.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.4 Lesson 2 — Truth table detectives, station 1: Setting out a truth table

questions.q: How many rows does a truth table need for an expression with four inputs?
questions.revisitLabel: 2.4 Lesson 2 — Truth table detectives, station 1: Setting out a truth table

questions.q: Explain why a truth table for four inputs has sixteen rows.

markPoints.exemplar: Each input can be either 0 or 1.

markPoints.concept: so the number of combinations is 2 multiplied by itself four times
markPoints.exemplar: So there are 2 to the power of 4, which is 16, combinations.

questions.example: Each of the four inputs can be either 0 or 1, so the number of different combinations is 2 × 2 × 2 × 2, which is 16.
questions.paraphrase: Every input takes one of two values, which means the total number of possibilities is two to the power of four, or sixteen.
questions.feedback: Two values each, multiplied together once per input.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.4 Lesson 2 — Truth table detectives, station 1: Setting out a truth table

questions.q: A truth table for two inputs has an output of 1 on exactly one row, where A = 1 and B = 1. Which expression does it describe?
questions.feedback: One row of 1, and it is the row where both inputs are 1. That is AND.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.4 Lesson 2 — Truth table detectives, station 1: Setting out a truth table

questions.q: A truth table for two inputs has an output of 1 on three rows and 0 only where A = 0 and B = 0. Which expression does it describe?
options: Q = NOT A OR NOT B
questions.feedback: OR is 0 only when every input is 0, which is the one row left.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.4 Lesson 2 — Truth table detectives, station 1: Setting out a truth table

questions.q: Explain why a truth table is a complete test of a logic circuit, when testing a program with every possible input is impossible.

markPoints.concept: a logic circuit has only a small fixed number of input combinations
markPoints.exemplar: A circuit with three inputs has only eight possible combinations.

markPoints.concept: so every one of them can be listed and checked
accept: list|listed|listing|write every one|write them down|written out|verified|verify|nothing left out|exhaustive|certain|tried
markPoints.exemplar: This means every single one can be listed and checked.

questions.example: Each input is either 0 or 1, so a circuit with three inputs has only eight possible combinations and one with four has sixteen. That is few enough to write every one down and check it, which is why a truth table proves a circuit works — a program taking a number could be given billions of values and never be tested exhaustively.
questions.paraphrase: Since every input can only be 0 or 1, the number of possibilities is tiny and fixed, so all of them can be written out and verified rather than sampled.
questions.feedback: How few combinations there are, and what being able to list them proves.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.4 Lesson 2 — Truth table detectives, station 1: Setting out a truth table

questions.q: How many rows does a truth table need for an expression with two inputs?
questions.feedback: Two inputs, two choices each: 2 times 2 is 4.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.4 Lesson 2 — Truth table detectives, station 4: Three inputs

questions.q: An expression has three inputs. A fourth input is added. What happens to the number of rows its truth table needs?
questions.feedback: Each new input has two possible values, and every existing row has to be written out for both of them. 8 becomes 16.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.4 Lesson 2 — Truth table detectives, station 4: Three inputs

questions.q: Sort each expression by how many inputs it has.
questions.feedback: Count the different letters, not the gates. NOT (A OR B) has two inputs and two gates.
